Case_Content:
Man, 64 years old, no significant medical history, presenting with a left colon tumor revealed by subocclusive syndrome.  Thoraco-abdominal CT scan shows a 6 cm colonic mass and two liver metastases in segments II and V measuring 2.2 and 3 cm. CEA: 120 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, MSS. No extra-hepatic disease.
MDT Discussion: Metastases considered primarily resectable, symptomatic colonic lesion is the priority.
Response:
Step 1 -  
- Resectability assessment: Resectable upfront.  
- Reasoning: The patient has a single, peripheral liver metastasis (segment VI, 2.5 cm) and no extra‑hepatic disease on PET. The primary ileocecal tumor is localized, and there is no evidence of extensive nodal disease or vascular involvement that would preclude simultaneous resection. The future liver remnant would be adequate after a segmental resection, and the patient’s age and lack of comorbidities make her a suitable surgical candidate.

Step 2 -  
- Pre‑operative work‑up:  
  - Confirm liver function (bilirubin, albumin, INR, platelet count).  
  - Obtain detailed staging of the primary tumor (T and N stage) via colonoscopy and MRI of the pelvis if needed.  
  - Review performance status (ECOG) and comorbidities.  
- Surgical plan:  
  - Perform a right hemicolectomy with ileocolic lymphadenectomy.  
  - Simultaneously resect the segment VI liver metastasis (wedge or segmentectomy) with clear margins.  
  - Consider minimally invasive approach if surgeon’s expertise and patient anatomy allow.  
- Post‑operative management:  
  - Early mobilisation and monitoring of liver function.  
  - Initiate adjuvant chemotherapy (e.g., 6 cycles of FOLFOX or CAPOX) once recovery permits, given the KRAS mutation and elevated CEA.  
  - Schedule surveillance imaging (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  
- Multidisciplinary review:  
  - Re‑evaluate response to adjuvant therapy and consider additional systemic therapy if residual disease or recurrence occurs.

Step 3 -  
- All essential clinical data for the primary tumor (location, size, T/N stage) and metastatic disease (number, size, location of liver lesions, CEA, KRAS status) are present; no further missing information is required for this recommendation.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient has a single 2.5 cm peripheral metastasis in segment VI, no radiologically evident extra hepatic disease, and the lesion is amenable to a non anatomic wedge resection with an expected R0 margin. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria, this pattern is considered to be potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution liver MRI and contrast enhanced CT to confirm absence of vascular/biliary involvement, evaluate arterial anatomy. Precise anatomic mapping is required to avoid intra operative surprise.

B. Systemic therapy
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab) because the tumor is KRAS mutated (no anti EGFR benefit).
• Re stage after chemotherapy with high resolution liver MRI (and contrast-enhanced CT).

C. Surgical management
• If restaging confirms continued resectability, perform a simultaneous right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) + a segment VI wedge/segmentectomy aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. (Simultaneous resection for solitary peripheral metastases is safe and oncologically equivalent to staged procedures 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.
• Alternative : consider two-stage surgical resection of primary and liver tumors / consider right hemicolectomy (standard oncologic resection of the right colon primary) with D2 lymphadectomy (at least 12 harvested lymph nodes) + an image-guided ablation using high-energy radio waves to generate heat via a probe (if no biliary or large vessels proximity)

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy (including the pre operative cycles). 
• Monitor CEA and imaging at 3 month intervals. A level of 35 ng/mL is acceptable but warrants close surveillance

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy. 
B. Potential extension of primary tumor to adjacent organ (abdominal wall, ureter, small bowel)
C. Detailed vascular/biliary relationship of the liver lesion – essential to confirm that a non anatomic resection will achieve clear margins without compromising hepatic inflow/outflow.
G. Patient’s nutritional status and postoperative recovery capacity, relevant for timing of chemotherapy.
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream
These items should be obtained before finalizing the operative plan.

Case_Content:
Man, 64 years old, no significant medical history, presenting with a left colon tumor revealed by subocclusive syndrome.  Thoraco-abdominal CT scan shows a 6 cm colonic mass and two liver metastases in segments II and V measuring 2.2 and 3 cm. CEA: 120 ng/mL. RAS wild-type, MSS. No extra-hepatic disease.
MDT Discussion: Metastases considered primarily resectable, symptomatic colonic lesion is the priority.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Resectable upfront.  
The patient has a single primary transverse colon adenocarcinoma with a high CEA but no evidence of obstructive symptoms or locally advanced disease on imaging. Three liver metastases (segments IV, V, VI) are 2–3 cm in diameter, are not invading the portal vein, and are amenable to a simple anatomic or wedge resection. There is no reported extra‑hepatic disease, and the anticipated future liver remnant would exceed the safe threshold (>2.5 L). Therefore, immediate surgical resection of both the primary and metastatic lesions is feasible without the need for pre‑operative downsizing or additional diagnostic work‑up.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Pre‑operative work‑up:  
   • Confirm performance status (ECOG 0–1), cardiopulmonary fitness, and baseline liver function tests.  
   • Obtain a detailed CT or MRI of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis to rule out occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
2. Operative plan: simultaneous resection of the transverse colon tumor (segmental colectomy with D3 lymphadenectomy) and the three liver metastases (segmental resections of IV, V, VI or a left lateral sectionectomy if anatomically convenient).  
3. Intra‑operative assessment of the future liver remnant and hemodynamics; use intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm margins.  
4. Post‑operative recovery: begin adjuvant chemotherapy 4–6 weeks after surgery.  
   • Standard regimen: 6 cycles of FOLFOX (oxaliplatin, leucovorin, 5‑FU) ± bevacizumab (given KRAS mutation, anti‑EGFR is not indicated).  
5. Surveillance:  
   • CEA measurement and contrast‑enhanced CT of the chest/abdomen every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months up to 5 years.  
   • Consider additional systemic therapy (e.g., FOLFOXIRI or addition of targeted agents) if recurrence occurs or if CEA rises.

Step 3 - Missing data  
No essential data are missing for the resectability assessment or the proposed surgical strategy. The following key information is already provided:  
• Primary tumor: transverse colon location, adenocarcinoma histology, CEA 410 ng/mL, no documented lymph node status (assumed resectable).  
• Metastatic disease: 3 lesions, 2–3 cm each, segments IV, V, VI, partial contact with right portal branch but no invasion, no extra‑hepatic disease reported.  
If any of the above points were uncertain (e.g., lymph node status, extra‑hepatic spread, liver function), they would need clarification before proceeding.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with three liver metastases located in segments IV, V, and VI (2–3 cm), confined to the right liver and central segments. MRI shows only partial contact with the right portal branch and no evidence of vascular invasion. These lesions appear technically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resections or anatomicalm resection while preserving adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number and size of metastases with preserved vascular structures, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative systemic therapy (strongly recommended)
• The very high CEA level (410 ng/mL) and KRAS mutation suggest biologically aggressive disease.
• Given the high CEA level (410 ng/mL), perform chest CT scan and high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT to assess extra-hepatic disease
• Administer 2–3 months of peri-operative doublet or triplet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI ± bevacizumab) to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control according to patient tolerance.
• This allows treatment of potential micrometastatic disease and assessment of tumor biology before surgery.

B. Restaging before surgery
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and contrast-enhanced CT after chemotherapy to reassess the relationship of the lesions to the right portal branch and confirm maintained resectability.
• Evaluate future liver remnant (FLR) if right hepatectomy of considered.

C. Surgical management (parenchymal-sparing strategy)
• If stability or response is observed, perform combined parenchymal-sparing resections guided by intra-operative ultrasound:
– Segment IV wedge/segmentectomy.
– Segment V and VI wedge resections.
• The goal is R0 resection while preserving maximal functional liver parenchyma and avoiding major hepatectomy.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins. 
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Management of the primary tumor
• Transverse colectomy of extended right colectomy with adequate oncologic margins and oncological lymphadenectomy with primary anastomosis.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for primary cancer resection.
• Otherwise, a staged approach with colectomy first is acceptable.

E. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging every 3 months given the high CEA level (410 ng/mL).

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Presence of potential extra-hepatic involvement on 18FDG PET-CT and chest CT scan.
B. Detailed vascular mapping on MRI to confirm absence of true portal invasion.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) calculation in case of right hepatectomy.F. Circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI, essential for rectal surgical planning. 
D. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
H. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Case_Content:
Woman, 56 years old, incidental discovery of a right colon tumor during a workup for iron deficiency anemia. Thoraco-Abdominal CT scan shows an ileocecal mass and a single 2.5 cm metastasis in segment VI. CEA 35 ng/mL, KRAS mutation present. No other lesions on FDG-PET.
MDT Discussion: Single peripheral metastasis, situation suitable for combined surgical treatment.
Response:
Step 1 -  
Resectability assessment: Resectable upfront.  
Reasoning: The patient has a T3N0 upper rectal carcinoma and three 1–2 cm liver metastases confined to segments VI, VII and VIII. The liver remnant (left lobe) will provide >30 % of total liver volume, and the patient’s liver function is presumed normal (no mention of cirrhosis or steatosis). The rectal tumor is amenable to a low anterior resection with total mesorectal excision, and the liver lesions can be removed in a single right trisegmentectomy. No additional downsizing therapy is required beyond the planned short‑course pelvic radiotherapy, which is part of the multimodality strategy rather than a prerequisite for resection.

Step 2 -  
Oncological strategy and surgical sequence:  

1. **Pre‑operative phase**  
   - Administer short‑course pelvic radiotherapy (5 × 5 Gy over 1 week) to the rectal tumor to reduce local tumor burden and improve sphincter preservation rates.  
   - Perform a baseline assessment of liver function (AST, ALT, bilirubin, INR, albumin) and calculate future liver remnant volume by volumetry.  
   - Evaluate performance status and comorbidities; optimize nutrition and anemia if present.  

2. **Surgical phase (combined approach)**  
   - **Day 1–2 post‑RT**: Proceed to a single‑stage laparoscopic or open procedure.  
   - **Right trisegmentectomy** (segments VI–VIII) with careful parenchymal transection, ensuring negative margins and adequate vascular control.  
   - **Low anterior resection** with total mesorectal excision and appropriate lymphadenectomy; consider sphincter‑preserving technique if the tumor is >5 cm from the anal verge.  
   - Intra‑operative assessment of liver remnant and hemodynamics; use Pringle maneuver if needed.  

3. **Post‑operative phase**  
   - Early mobilisation, pain control, and monitoring of liver function.  
   - Initiate adjuvant chemotherapy (CAPOX or FOLFOX) 4–6 weeks post‑operatively for 6 months, given RAS wild‑type status and high CEA.  
   - Continue CEA monitoring and imaging surveillance (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis) every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.  

Step 3 -  
Missing data that would refine the recommendation:  

- Detailed liver function tests (AST, ALT, bilirubin, INR, albumin) and assessment of hepatic steatosis or fibrosis.  
- Precise future liver remnant volume and liver volumetry data.  
- Performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky) and comorbidities (cardiac, pulmonary, renal).  
- Exact distance of the rectal tumour from the anal verge and sphincter involvement.  
- Baseline CEA trend and any evidence of occult extra‑hepatic disease on MRI or PET/CT beyond the reported findings.  
- Patient preference regarding sphincter preservation and willingness for combined surgery.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with three small liver metastases (1–2 cm) located in segments VI, VII, and VIII, without evidence of extrahepatic disease. Although confined to the right liver, the lesions seem technically amenable to parenchymal-sparing resections with preservation of an adequate future liver remnant. According to current hepatobiliary oncologic criteria for limited number, small size, and favorable location of metastases, this pattern is considered potentially resectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Preoperative staging
• Obtain high resolution pelvic MRI and contrast enhanced CT to confirm primary tumor location, circumferential and distal margins, lymph nodes involvement, invasion of fascia recti. A chest CT scan for extrahepatic disease.

B. Systemic therapy
• Give 2–3 months of peri operative doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX ± bevacizumab or cetuximab)
• RAS wild-type status allows consideration of anti-EGFR therapy depending on MDT strategy.
• Re stage after chemotherapy with high resolution liver and pelvic MRI (and contrast-enhanced CT) to assess tumor biology and optimize oncologic control for both primary tumor and liver metastases

C. Management of the rectal primary (oncologic priority)
• Given the T3N0 upper rectal cancer, long-course radiotherapy is appropriate to optimize local control and allow coordinated surgical planning.

D. Coordinated surgical strategy
• Initiate doublet chemotherapy (FOLFOX or CAPOX) during the waiting period following radiotherapy. This period treats potential micrometastatic disease and tests tumor biology.
• Consider image-guided ablation of the three lesions using high-energy radio waves to generate heat via a probe (if no biliary or large vessels proximity)
• After restaging with high-resolution liver MRI and pelvic imaging,
-	If complete morphological rectal tumor response : resection / ablation of the segments VI, VII and VIII metastases with follow up of primary tumor
-	If near complete morphological rectal tumor response : resection / ablation of the segments VI, VII and VIII metastases followed with strict follow up of primary tumor
-	If incomplete morphological rectal tumor response : liver-first resection or ablation of the segments VI, VII and VIII metastases, then rectal resection after appropriate recovery, using a staged or synchronous strategy : oncologic resection of the upper rectum (low anterior resection with TME principles).
– Parenchymal-sparing segment III wedge/segmentectomy aiming for ≥1 mm R0 margin.
• Use intra operative ultrasound to verify lesion location and margins.
• Ideally, consider minimally invasive approach (laparoscopic or robotic) for liver resection.

D. Postoperative therapy
• Pathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete a total of 6 months of systemic chemotherapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close surveillance with CEA and imaging at 3-month intervals.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A.	Exact distance of the rectal tumor from the anal verge, and circumferential resection margin (CRM) status on pelvic MRI influencing surgical approach and anastomotic risk
B.	A chest CT scan for extrahepatic disease
B. Detailed vascular and biliary relationships of the three liver lesions on MRI.
C. Grade of differentiation and MSS/ MSI mutation of the primary tumor : influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
F. Liquid biopsies to search circulating tumor DNA (ctDNA) and circulating tumor cells (CTCs) in the bloodstream

Man, 68 years old, history of smoking, presenting with T3N1 upper rectal adenocarcinoma with a single 1.8 cm liver metastasis in segment III. Pelvic MRI: limited parietal invasion. CEA 45 ng/mL. RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Single resectable metastasis, possibility of coordinated surgical treatment after short-course radiotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
- Resectable upfront  
  - The patient has a single primary sigmoid colon tumor (T3N1) and two contiguous liver metastases confined to segment VI, each <3 cm.  
  - Imaging shows no extra‑hepatic disease, no vascular invasion, and adequate future liver remnant (>30 % in a healthy liver).  
  - The lesions are accessible and can be removed with a segmental resection or wedge excision without major vascular sacrifice.  
  - No contraindication to simultaneous resection of the colon and liver lesions is evident, and the MDT has ruled out the need for neoadjuvant chemotherapy.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Pre‑operative work‑up  
   - Confirm normal liver function (bilirubin, transaminases, albumin, INR).  
   - Verify performance status (ECOG 0‑1) and absence of comorbidities that would preclude major surgery.  
   - Obtain a detailed CT or MRI of the liver to delineate the exact margins of the metastases and plan the resection.  
2. Operative plan (synchronous)  
   - Perform a sigmoid colectomy with adequate lymphadenectomy and primary anastomosis (low anterior resection or sigmoidectomy).  
   - Immediately after colon resection, proceed to the liver: perform a segment VI wedge or segmentectomy, ensuring negative margins and adequate parenchymal preservation.  
   - Use intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm no additional occult lesions.  
3. Post‑operative management  
   - Early mobilisation, pain control, and monitoring of liver function.  
   - Initiate adjuvant chemotherapy 4–6 weeks post‑operatively with a standard oxaliplatin‑based regimen (FOLFOX or CAPOX) for 6 months, given the KRAS mutation and high CEA.  
   - Consider adding bevacizumab if clinically indicated and tolerated.  
4. Surveillance  
   - CEA every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.  
   - CT abdomen/pelvis every 6 months for 2 years, then annually.  
   - PET/CT if recurrence suspected.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- Detailed liver function tests and hepatic reserve assessment.  
- Complete staging imaging (CT chest, PET/CT) to rule out occult extra‑hepatic disease.  
- Precise measurements of the primary tumor (distance from anal verge, size).  
- Patient’s ECOG performance status and comorbidities.  
- Prior abdominal surgeries or adhesions that might affect operative approach.  
- Planned adjuvant chemotherapy regimen and patient’s tolerance.

   - Resect the segment VII lesion via a wedge or formal segmentectomy, ensuring a 1‑cm margin and negative margins confirmed by frozen section.

   - Early recovery with monitoring of liver function and drain output.  
   - Initiate adjuvant chemotherapy (e.g., 6 cycles of CAPOX or FOLFOX) within 4–6 weeks post‑op, tailored to the patient’s tolerance.  
   - For RAS‑wild‑type disease, consider anti‑EGFR therapy (cetuximab or panitumumab) in case of recurrence or progression.  
   - Schedule surveillance imaging (CT chest/abdomen) every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.

- Primary tumor staging (T and N status).  
- Presence or absence of peritoneal carcinomatosis or other extra‑hepatic metastases.  
- Detailed liver function assessment (Child‑Pugh score, ICG clearance).  
- Liver volumetry and future liver remnant estimation.

A prerequisite for surgical resection is systemic chemotherapy to downsize the disease and potentially convert the case to a resectable state. No other decisive missing information precludes this classification.

Step 2 -  
Oncological strategy  

1. Baseline assessment  
   - Confirm that the primary transverse colon tumor is technically resectable (no obstruction, perforation, or unresectable local invasion).  
   - Obtain baseline liver function tests (bilirubin, albumin, INR) and calculate future liver remnant (FLR) volume on CT volumetry.  
   - Document performance status and comorbidities.

2. Systemic chemotherapy  
   - Initiate first-line FOLFOX + bevacizumab (or FOLFIRI + bevacizumab if oxaliplatin intolerance) for 4–6 cycles.  
   - Monitor CEA levels and repeat liver MRI/CT after 2–3 cycles to assess radiologic response.  
   - If disease progression or unacceptable toxicity occurs, switch to second-line FOLFIRI + bevacizumab or consider clinical trial enrollment.

3. Re‑evaluation for resectability  
   - After chemotherapy, re‑assess tumor burden, FLR, and any new extrahepatic disease.  
   - If lesions have shrunk or become confined to one lobe with adequate FLR, plan for synchronous resection of primary and liver metastases.  
   - If lesions remain bilobar and major hepatectomy would leave insufficient FLR, proceed to a staged approach.

4. Staged liver resection (if required)  
   - Stage 1: Resection of lesions in one lobe (e.g., right or left) and portal vein embolization (PVE) of the contralateral lobe to induce hypertrophy.  
   - Stage 2: After ≥4–6 weeks and sufficient hypertrophy (FLR > 30–35% in normal liver, >40% in diseased liver), perform completion hepatectomy of remaining lesions.  
   - Consider intraoperative ablation (RFA/MWA) for small lesions adjacent to major vessels that are technically difficult to resect.

5. Primary tumor resection  
   - Perform right hemicolectomy with D3 lymphadenectomy, either concurrently with liver surgery (if safe) or in a separate operation after liver resection.  
   - Ensure adequate margins and lymph node harvest.

6. Postoperative management  
   - Resume adjuvant chemotherapy (FOLFOX or FOLFIRI + bevacizumab) for 6 months, unless contraindicated by recovery.  
   - Monitor CEA and imaging every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months for years 3–5.

7. Contingency plans  
   - If conversion fails or disease progresses during chemotherapy, consider alternative systemic regimens, targeted agents (e.g., regorafenib, TAS-102), or enrollment in clinical trials.  
   - If liver function or FLR remains inadequate, evaluate for liver transplantation in selected cases (rare for colorectal metastases) or palliative systemic therapy.

Step 3 -  
Missing essential data that would refine the recommendation:  

- Patient’s ECOG performance status and detailed comorbidity profile (cardiopulmonary, renal).  
- Complete liver function panel (bilirubin, albumin, INR, AST/ALT, alkaline phosphatase).  
- Precise volumetric assessment of future liver remnant and total liver volume.  
- Detailed mapping of each liver lesion (size, exact location relative to hepatic veins, proximity to biliary ducts).  
- Presence or absence of extrahepatic disease beyond the liver (e.g., peritoneal implants, lung nodules).  
- Trend of CEA levels over time and response to initial chemotherapy.  
- Details of the primary tumor (size, depth of invasion, perforation, obstruction).

Resectable upfront. The two lesions (2.8 cm in segment V and 3.2 cm in segment VIII) are anatomically accessible, there is no evidence of extra‑hepatic disease, and the patient is in good general condition. No downsizing chemotherapy or additional diagnostic information is required before proceeding to surgery.

Oncological strategy  

1. **Pre‑operative assessment**  
   - Full liver function panel (bilirubin, ALT/AST, albumin, INR, platelet count).  
   - Volumetric MRI or CT to calculate future liver remnant (FLR); FLR should be ≥30 % of total liver volume (or ≥40 % if underlying liver disease).  
   - Performance status (ECOG 0‑1) and comorbidity review.  
   - Baseline CEA and other tumor markers.  

2. **Peri‑operative chemotherapy**  
   - Administer 3 cycles of FOLFOX (or CAPOX) as neoadjuvant therapy to reduce micrometastatic disease and assess chemosensitivity.  
   - Re‑evaluate CEA and imaging after 3 cycles to confirm stability or response.  

3. **Surgical resection**  
   - Perform an anatomic resection of segments V and VIII with at least a 1‑cm margin.  
   - Intra‑operative ultrasound to confirm lesion boundaries and exclude occult disease.  
   - Ensure adequate FLR and hemostasis; consider intra‑operative portal vein embolization only if FLR is borderline.  

4. **Post‑operative management**  
   - Resume adjuvant chemotherapy with 3 additional cycles of FOLFOX (or CAPOX) once the patient recovers from surgery.  
   - Monitor liver function and CEA during chemotherapy.  

5. **Surveillance**  
   - CEA and liver‑function tests every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months.  
   - Contrast‑enhanced CT or MRI of the liver and chest every 6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  
   - Prompt evaluation of any new symptoms or rising CEA.

- Detailed liver function tests (bilirubin, albumin, INR, platelet count).  
- Precise future liver remnant volume and assessment of underlying liver disease or steatosis.  
- Complete performance status and comorbidity profile.  
- Prior systemic therapy details (if any) and CEA trend over time.  
- Imaging of other potential metastatic sites (e.g., chest CT, PET‑CT) to confirm absence of extra‑hepatic disease.  
- Genetic profile beyond KRAS/BRAF (e.g., MSI status, NTRK, HER2).

  • Perform an isolated segment VI liver resection (open or laparoscopic depending on surgeon preference and intra‑operative findings).  
  • Ensure negative margins (R0 resection) and adequate future liver remnant (>30% in a normal liver).

  • Initiate adjuvant systemic chemotherapy (e.g., 6 cycles of FOLFOX) starting 4–6 weeks after recovery, given the high CEA and KRAS mutation.  
  • Monitor CEA levels monthly for the first 6 months, then every 3 months for 2 years.  
  • Schedule surveillance imaging (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis) every 3 months for the first 2 years, then every 6 months up to 5 years.  
- Long‑term follow‑up  
  • Continue routine surveillance for recurrence; consider second‑line systemic therapy if recurrence occurs, noting KRAS status limits anti‑EGFR options.

Woman, 60 years old, T3N1M1 sigmoid tumor, four bilobar liver metastases (segments II, III, VI, VIII) with one in contact with the right hepatic vein at the thoraco-abdominal CT scan. CEA 240 ng/mL. RAS wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Bilobar involvement for conversion, imaging to be re-evaluated after 4 cycles of chemotherapy.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable.  
- The patient has a single cerebellar metastasis that requires urgent neurosurgical or stereotactic radiosurgical treatment before any systemic or hepatic intervention can be safely undertaken.  
- Multiple bilobar liver metastases are present; given the extent, a single‑stage resection would likely leave an insufficient future liver remnant, and down‑staging chemotherapy is required to assess resectability.  
- Therefore, definitive hepatic resection can only be considered after brain disease control and systemic therapy response evaluation.

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
1. Neurological priority:  
   - Perform stereotactic radiosurgery or craniotomy with resection of the cerebellar metastasis, with peri‑operative steroids as needed.  
   - Obtain post‑treatment MRI to confirm local control.  
2. Systemic therapy:  
   - Initiate first‑line chemotherapy (e.g., FOLFOX + bevacizumab or FOLFIRI + bevacizumab) tailored to RAS/BRAF status; consider adding a targeted agent if RAS‑wild type.  
   - Administer 3–4 cycles, then reassess with contrast‑enhanced CT of chest, abdomen, pelvis and brain MRI.  
3. Re‑evaluation of hepatic disease:  
   - If imaging shows a reduction in tumor burden and the future liver remnant is adequate (>25–30% in normal liver, >40–50% in diseased liver), plan for curative liver resection.  
   - If lesions remain bilobar and resection is not feasible, consider a two‑stage hepatectomy or ALPPS, or continue systemic therapy with possible conversion to resection.  
4. Primary colon tumor:  
   - If the primary is asymptomatic, defer resection until after systemic therapy and brain control.  
   - If obstruction, perforation risk, or significant bleeding is present, perform right hemicolectomy (or segmental resection) either concurrently with liver resection or after systemic therapy.  
5. Post‑operative management:  
   - Resume adjuvant chemotherapy for 6–9 months, monitoring CEA and imaging.  
   - Continue surveillance with CEA, CT scans, and MRI of the brain every 3–6 months for the first 2 years, then annually.  
6. Multidisciplinary coordination:  
   - Regular MDT meetings to review response, adjust therapy, and plan subsequent interventions.

Step 3 - Missing data  
- RAS, BRAF, and MSI status of the primary tumor.  
- Detailed liver volumetry and future liver remnant assessment.  
- Size, exact location, and number of liver lesions.  
- Primary tumor symptoms (obstruction, bleeding, perforation risk).  
- Performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky).  
- Baseline liver function tests and comorbidities.  
- Prior treatments (if any) and tolerance.  
- Detailed neurological assessment and post‑treatment MRI of the cerebellar metastasis.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with multiple bilobar liver metastases associated with a cerebellar metastasis in the context of a right T4N2 colon cancer and markedly elevated CEA (860 ng/mL). The presence of brain metastasis indicates advanced systemic dissemination and excludes any curative hepatobiliary surgical strategy at this stage. From a hepatobiliary perspective, this situation is considered unresectable.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Neurological priority (mandatory)
• Immediate neurosurgical and/or radiotherapy assessment of the cerebellar metastasis is required as the first therapeutic step.
• The objective is neurological control and symptom prevention.

B. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI and thoraco-abdominal CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of liver lesions
• Calculate the future liver remnant (FLR).
• Given the high CEA level (860 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

C. Systemic therapy after neurological stabilization
• Initiate or adapt systemic chemotherapy according to MDT decision once neurological status is stabilized.
• The objective is global disease control.

D. Radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-quality liver MRI and full-body imaging after 2–3 months to evaluate response.
• Monitor CEA kinetics.

E. Criteria for reconsidering liver-directed therapy (exceptional)
• Hepatobiliary surgical re-evaluation would be considered only in the rare situation of complete neurological control and major hepatic response, which remains highly unlikely.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Neurological status and resectability of the cerebellar metastasis.
B. Exact segmental distribution and vascular relationships of liver lesions.
D. Molecular profile to optimize systemic treatment.
E. Status and symptoms related to the primary colon tumor.
F. Presence or absence of additional extrahepatic disease on full staging.
G. Radiologic tumor response after systemic chemotherapy (decrease, stability or progression) and evolution of CEA.

Case_Content:
Man, 63 years old, left T4N2M1 colon cancer, multiple liver metastases (≥8 lesions), maximum size 4.5 cm, partial contact with the IVC at the abdominal CT scan. CEA 890 ng/mL. BRAF wild-type.
MDT Discussion: Extensive liver disease, potentially resectable after major response to FOLFOXIRI.
Response:
Step 1 - Resectability assessment  
Potentially resectable – the patient has extensive bilobar liver disease and pulmonary micronodules that preclude immediate curative resection. A prerequisite is systemic chemotherapy (and possibly neoadjuvant chemoradiation for the rectal tumor) to downsize the disease and assess response before any surgical intervention can be considered.  

Step 2 - Oncological strategy  
- Initiate first‑line systemic therapy with a RAS‑wild‑type–appropriate regimen: FOLFOX + bevacizumab or FOLFIRI + cetuximab, depending on institutional preference and patient comorbidities.  
- Concurrently plan short‑course chemoradiation for the rectal tumor (e.g., 5‑FU or capecitabine with 45–50.4 Gy) to achieve local control and potentially downstage the primary.  
- Re‑evaluate after 3–4 cycles of chemotherapy:  
  • Repeat CT chest/abdomen/pelvis and CEA measurement.  
  • Assess radiologic response of liver lesions (≥30 % reduction in sum diameter) and pulmonary nodules.  
  • If response is adequate and the patient’s performance status remains good, proceed to a staged surgical approach:  
    – First, perform a curative resection of the rectal tumor (low anterior resection or abdominoperineal resection) with appropriate lymphadenectomy.  
    – Second, evaluate the liver for resectability; if a sufficient future liver remnant (>30 % in normal liver, >40 % in diseased liver) can be achieved, perform a two‑stage hepatectomy or associating liver partition and portal vein ligation for staged hepatectomy (ALPPS) if rapid hypertrophy is needed.  
    – Third, if pulmonary micronodules persist but are limited in number (<5) and accessible, consider stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) or surgical metastasectomy after systemic therapy.  
- Throughout the course, monitor CEA trends, liver function tests, and patient tolerance.  
- If disease progression occurs before surgical candidacy, consider second‑line systemic therapy (e.g., FOLFOX + panitumumab or FOLFIRI + panitumumab) and reassess for local ablative options (RFA, microwave ablation) for liver lesions that are not amenable to resection.  

Step 3 - Missing data  
Essential clinical data that remain unknown and would refine the management plan:  
- Exact size and number of each liver metastasis and pulmonary micronodule.  
- Detailed performance status (ECOG/Karnofsky).  
- Baseline liver function (bilirubin, albumin, INR, Child‑Pugh score).  
- Cardiac and pulmonary reserve (spirometry, echocardiogram).  
- Prior history of chemotherapy or radiotherapy.  
- Patient preferences regarding aggressive multimodality treatment versus palliative care.
Reference:
Step 1 – Resectability assessment
The patient presents with six bilobar liver metastases and pulmonary micronodules in the context of a T4N2 rectal tumor and very high CEA (1250 ng/mL). The combination of extensive bilobar hepatic disease and extrahepatic pulmonary involvement reflects advanced systemic dissemination. From a hepatobiliary perspective, this situation is considered unresectable upfront.

Step 2 – Recommended oncologic sequence
A. Comprehensive staging and multidisciplinary planning
• Perform high-resolution liver and pelvic MRI and chest CT to confirm exact number, distribution, and resectability of both liver and lung lesions.
• Thoracic surgical assessment of pulmonary nodules is required.
• Given the high CEA level (1250 ng/mL) and multifocal metastases, perform high-resolution 18FDG PET-CT

B. Initial systemic therapy (mandatory)
• Start systemic chemotherapy (FOLFOX/FOLFIRI ± anti-EGFR given RAS wild-type status).
• The objective is to assess tumor biology and confirm disease control at hepatic and pulmonary sites.

C. Close radiologic reassessment
• Perform high-resolution liver MRI, and thoraco-abdominal enhanced CT-scan every 2-3 months to evaluate response and detect any potential reduction in tumor burden that could open a limited local treatment window.
• Monitor CEA kinetics as a marker of treatment effect.

D. Criteria for secondary resectability
• Surgery can be considered only if chemotherapy induces:
– Significant reduction in lesion size and number in both liver and lung.
– Feasibility of staged or parenchymal-sparing resections with adequate future liver remnant.

E. Potential surgical strategies for liver metastases if response is favorable
• Hepatobiliary surgical re-evaluation would be considered only in the rare case of major response with significant reduction of both hepatic and pulmonary disease, allowing complete clearance of all sites.
• Two-stage hepatectomy or combined parenchymal-sparing resections depending on response pattern.
• Portal vein embolization / venous deprivation / ALPPS may be required if major hepatectomy becomes necessary.

F. Pelvic management integration
• Plan rectal treatment (short-course radiotherapy or chemoradiotherapy) according the MDT discussion if the primary tumor is symptomatic

G. If insufficient response and if disease remains disseminated
• Continue second-line systemic therapy according to MDT, and consider palliative or symptom-oriented strategies according to MDT.

H. Postoperative therapy and surveillance
• If resection, analysis ofpathology report : confirmation of tumor type and origin, immunohistochemistry with tumor markers, histological growth pattern, margin status (R0, R1, R2), tumor grade, differentiation, pathologic response score (TRG), necrosis/fibrosis
• Complete approximately 6 months of systemic therapy including pre-operative cycles.
• Close follow-up with CEA and imaging of both liver and lungs.

Step 3 – Critical missing information
A. Exact segmental distribution and vascular relationships of the liver metastases.
B. Characterization of pulmonary micronodules on chest CT.
C. Future liver remnant (FLR) estimation.
D. Status and symptoms related to the primary rectum tumor : detailed pelvic MRI to plan rectal treatment.
E. Patient’s performance status for staged multimodal procedures.
F. Confirmation of absence of other extrahepatic disease on full staging.
G. Evolution of CEA and radiologic response over time.
H. Grade of differentiation, MSS/ MSI mutation and molecular status of the primary cancer: influences prognosis and need for intensified adjuvant therapy
